title: 1. Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Stock Cycles

epigraph.quote: In biopharma, curing a disease is the highest form of medical triumph and the fastest way to shrink your own addressable market—unless you build a platform that outlives any single molecule.
epigraph.author: Institutional Biotech Underwriting Maxim

web_blocks.html: Dr. Michael Riordan founded Gilead Sciences in June 1987 in Foster City, California [1]. At age 29, the doctor-turned-venture-investor licensed antisense chemistry to block viral RNA and DNA growth [1]. When Gilead went public in January 1992, it had no revenue and burned cash on nucleotide research. Its first real breakthrough came not from gene silencing, but from small-molecule antiviral drugs. These molecules mimic the building blocks of viral DNA and halt replication. That chemistry led to Vistide for CMV retinitis in 1996 and Tamiflu (with Hoffmann-La Roche) for flu in 1999. Most importantly, it produced Viread (TDF) in 2001. In 2003, Gilead bought Triangle Pharmaceuticals for $464 million to pair TDF with emtricitabine (FTC), launching Truvada in 2004 and Atripla in 2006 [1].

That single-tablet regimen (STR) combined three active HIV drugs into one daily pill. It turned HIV from a fatal illness requiring handfuls of toxic pills into a chronic disease. Patients took their medicine far more reliably when one pill replaced complex multi-drug schedules. It also built Gilead's core economic engine: high virology share and ~80%–86% product gross margins. Selling costs stayed low because HIV clinics and Ryan White / 340B buyers are concentrated [1]. Later, Gilead upgraded its core backbone from TDF to tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) and added bictegravir to launch Biktarvy in 2018. Over the past 15 years, Gilead's history has followed three capital cycles. Each cycle shows both strong virology science and uneven results in outside M&A.

web_blocks.takeaway: Gilead's $11B Pharmasset bet remains one of biopharma's greatest deals, whereas its 2017–2020 oncology spree ($37.8B across Kite, Forty Seven, and Immunomedics) produced severe capital-efficiency drag; post-2024 bolt-ons (CymaBay, Arcellx) reflect tighter clinical derisking.

web_blocks.html: The first cycle was the Hepatitis C (HCV) boom from 2014 to 2016. In November 2011, Gilead paid $11.0 billion for Pharmasset, a deal many critics called reckless. That bet secured sofosbuvir, the core drug behind Sovaldi (2013), Harvoni (2014), and Epclusa (2016). Cure rates jumped above 95% in 8 to 12 weeks without harsh interferon shots. Revenue surged from $11.2 billion in 2013 to $32.6 billion in 2015, and operating cash flow topped $17 billion in 2016. Then the cure paradox hit. As Gilead cured millions of patients and AbbVie launched Mavyret, HCV sales fell fast. Total revenue dropped from $30.39 billion in 2016 to $22.13 billion in 2018 [1].

The second cycle was the 2017–2021 diversification push and COVID-19 windfall. Seeking a second growth leg beyond HIV and shrinking HCV, Gilead bought Kite Pharma for $11.9 billion in 2017 [13]. In March 2019, it hired Roche veteran Daniel O'Day as Chairman and CEO. O'Day set a bold goal to make cancer drugs one-third of Gilead's revenue by 2030. To speed up that shift, Gilead spent $25.9 billion in 2020 alone. It paid $4.9 billion for Forty Seven (magrolimab) and $21.0 billion for Immunomedics (Trodelvy) [12]. At the same time, its antiviral Veklury (remdesivir) became a standard hospital COVID-19 drug, hitting $5.6 billion in 2021 sales and masking weak core growth. Later, Veklury faded to $1.8 billion in 2024, $911 million in 2025 [3], and ~$300 million projected in 2026 [4]. That drop exposed Gilead's cancer M&A missteps. Magrolimab failed in MDS/AML trials and was dropped, while Trodelvy's lung and bladder setbacks forced a $2.4 billion write-down in 2024 [19].

The third cycle, from 2024 to 2026, marks a return to Gilead's core strength in long-acting virology, paired with sharper late-stage deals. In HIV, the capsid blocker lenacapavir achieved 100% efficacy in cisgender women (PURPOSE-1) [6]. It also showed ≥99.9% protection in men and gender-diverse groups (PURPOSE-2) [7]. The FDA approved it as twice-yearly PrEP (Yeztugo) on June 18, 2025 [5]. Meanwhile, Gilead settled patent suits to push U.S. Biktarvy generics from December 2033 to April 1, 2036 [14]. It will also absorb a 38% Medicare Maximum Fair Price cut under the IRA starting January 1, 2028 [15]. In liver and cancer care, the $4.3 billion CymaBay deal brought in Livdelzi [11]. Trodelvy won key first-line mTNBC approvals in June 2026 [8], and Gilead paid $7.8 billion in April 2026 for Arcellx to own anito-cel [9, 10].

web_blocks.title: Cycle Lesson: Virological Craftsmanship vs. M&A Hubris
paragraphs: Over nearly four decades, Gilead's internal chemistry—tenofovir, bictegravir, sofosbuvir, and lenacapavir—has built lasting market leaders. By contrast, buying early cancer assets at peak prices without Phase 3 survival proof (Forty Seven, Immunomedics) led to heavy GAAP write-downs. Separating the steady virology cash engine from the M&A record is the core task of this audit.

book_paragraphs: If you want to understand Gilead Sciences without getting lost in biotech jargon, you and I should start with a paradox that sits at the heart of its 39-year history. In 1987, a 29-year-old physician named Michael Riordan started Gilead in Foster City, California, with a simple conviction: if you can design small molecules that look like the natural building blocks of DNA and RNA, you can trick a virus into stopping its own replication. That single chemical insight turned Gilead into one of the most profitable drugmakers on earth. Yet it also taught the company a brutal lesson about pharmaceutical economics: when your chemistry is so good that it cures a chronic disease, you literally cure your own revenue stream out of existence.

To see how that played out, walk with me through three distinct acts. Act One was the HIV empire and the Hepatitis C supernova. In 2001, Gilead launched Viread, and two years later paid just $464 million for Triangle Pharmaceuticals to combine tenofovir with emtricitabine into Truvada. By 2006, Gilead had compressed a terrifying multi-pill HIV regimen into a single daily tablet, Atripla. Every few years thereafter, Gilead upgraded the chemical backbone—replacing toxic older molecules with tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) and later pairing it with the integrase inhibitor bictegravir to launch Biktarvy in 2018. Biktarvy did not just win the HIV market; it owned it, climbing to more than half of all U.S. HIV prescriptions.

Meanwhile, in late 2011, Gilead made a bet that looked reckless to Wall Street at the time: it paid $11 billion in cash for Pharmasset, a clinical-stage biotech with a Hepatitis C nucleotide analog called sofosbuvir. Within four years, Sovaldi and Harvoni turned Hepatitis C from a slow, liver-destroying death sentence into an eight-to-twelve-week oral cure with 95%-plus efficacy. Gilead's revenue nearly tripled from $11.2 billion in 2013 to $32.6 billion in 2015, and operating cash flow hit $17.05 billion in 2016. Then the paradox struck. Once Gilead cured millions of diagnosed patients—and AbbVie arrived with a cheaper competing cure—Hepatitis C sales fell off a cliff. Total revenue dropped by more than $10 billion between 2015 and 2018, and Gilead spent the next five years searching for a second act.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Notice the pattern as we move from Act One to Act Two: Gilead is phenomenal when it compounds inside its core virology competency, and far more vulnerable when it pays peak-cycle prices to buy its way into unfamiliar oncology biology.

book_subsections.title: Act Two: The Oncology Buying Spree and the Pandemic Mirage (2017–2023)
paragraphs: Act Two began in August 2017 with an $11.9 billion acquisition of Kite Pharma, bringing autologous CAR-T cell therapy into Gilead's fold just before Yescarta won FDA approval for aggressive lymphoma. In March 2019, Gilead hired Daniel O'Day away from Roche to run the company, and O'Day wasted no time setting a bold strategic marker: oncology would grow to represent one-third of Gilead's revenue by 2030.

In 2020, O'Day backed that ambition with $25.9 billion of M&A in a single calendar year. First came Forty Seven in March 2020 for $4.9 billion, a bet on an anti-CD47 antibody called magrolimab that was supposed to unleash macrophages against blood cancers. Seven months later came Immunomedics for $21 billion, securing Trodelvy, an antibody-drug conjugate targeting Trop-2. On paper, Gilead suddenly had a flagship cell therapy, a flagship ADC, and a novel innate-immunity checkpoint.

In reality, the next four years tested management's credibility. Just as those deals closed, COVID-19 struck, and Gilead's broad-spectrum antiviral remdesivir—branded Veklury—became the standard hospitalized treatment worldwide, peaking at $5.6 billion in 2021. Veklury's windfall masked what was happening under the hood in oncology: magrolimab suffered FDA clinical holds and fatal overall-survival failures, ending in a full program write-off; Trodelvy failed confirmatory trials in bladder cancer and non-small cell lung cancer, forcing a $2.4 billion impairment charge in 2024; and Kite's cell therapy growth stalled as Bristol Myers Squibb's Breyanzi and J&J's Carvykti gained ground.

book_subsections.title: Act Three: Back to Virology Mastery and Disciplined Bolt-Ons (2024–2026)
paragraphs: Act Three—the chapter Gilead is writing right now in 2025 and 2026—looks far more coherent, precisely because it returned to Gilead's unmatched virology engine while fixing the clinical bar on external deals. In the lab, Gilead's chemists cracked one of HIV's hardest structural problems: targeting the viral capsid protein, which protects HIV's genetic material. The result was lenacapavir, a molecule so potent and long-acting that a single subcutaneous injection protects against HIV acquisition for six full months.

When the Phase 3 PURPOSE-1 trial reported 100% efficacy—zero infections among more than 2,100 women in South Africa and Uganda—and PURPOSE-2 confirmed 99.9%-plus protection in men and gender-diverse participants, the FDA approved Yeztugo in June 2025. By Q3 2026, Yeztugo was already running at a $1 billion annualized pace. At the same time, Gilead's legal team settled with generic challengers to extend Biktarvy's U.S. patent protection out to April 2036, even as the federal government selected Biktarvy for a 38% Medicare price cut starting in 2028.

Even the non-HIV businesses began clicking in 2024–2026. The $4.3 billion CymaBay acquisition delivered Livdelzi, which surged 93% year-over-year in Q3 2026 to $203 million. Trodelvy redeemed part of its Immunomedics price tag in June 2026 by winning FDA approval in first-line metastatic triple-negative breast cancer, jumping 42% in Q3 2026 to $506 million. And in April 2026, Gilead closed a $7.8 billion acquisition of Arcellx to own 100% of anito-cel, a next-generation multiple myeloma CAR-T awaiting an FDA decision on December 23, 2026. The lesson for you and me is clear: Gilead's scientific engine is back in rhythm, but its GAAP financial statements still carry the scars of its $12.4 billion 2026 IPR&D bill and past oncology write-downs.
